newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Political bickering hits Zimbabwe privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Political bickering hits Zimbabwe privatisation.

text.p: Political bickering over investment opportunities is delaying Zimbabwe's long-awaited privatisation programme, local economic and political analysts said on Wednesday.

Controversy over government tender awards, and accusations that some business and political elites have hijacked the drive to empower the black majority, are damaging the southern African country's investment profile, they said.

After a 10-year experiment with socialism, President Robert Mugabe's government committed itself over seven years ago to a scheme to break up monopolies and to commercialise and privatise dozens of mostly loss-making state enterprises.

But for five years it set no policy and pursued the scheme at a pace which some economic analysts saw as largely aimed at staving off criticism from Western donors seeking economic reforms sponsored by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Zimbabwe's sales of state assets raised a mere U.S.$59 million in the financial year ended June 1996 against a target of $2.3 billion.

The government says it has now found its footing, and Mugabe has been telling potential foreign investors that he will speed up privatisation while maintaining its core aim of economically empowering the country's majority black people.

Privatisation receipts are projected to total Z$1 billion ($89 million) in the current financial year, but many analysts believe the government cannot meet the target and it still has to undertake the promised large-scale reform or privatisation of the public sector.
"Things have been painfully slow but the process will be even slower now with all these controversies," said John Robertson, a leading private economic consultant.

He was referring to controversy surrounding the government's recent decision to award the country's first private cellular phone licence to a consortium of black businessmen, including President Mugabe's nephew Leo Mugabe, and a foreign firm called Telecel.

Many Zimbabweans expected the licence to go to Econet, a Zimbabwean company led by Strive Masiyiwa, which has been battling the state in the courts for the last three years for the licence and has already set up a system which is ready to start.

The government denies public accusations that it favoured Telecel, but the award has been temporarily suspended by the state tender board to allow the ministry of information, posts and telecommunications to reply "point by point" to complaints lodged by Econet in a 100-page document, and other bidders.
The cellular phone tender has left President Robert Mugabe's cabinet bickering and its business allies in the black economic empowerment campaign highly divided and supporting different bidders.

"It's a dog fight over opportunities...and we are going to move very slowly (towards privatisation) in these circumstances," said John Makumbe, a political scientist at Harare's University of Zimbabwe.

The failure of Zimbabwe's political process -- dominated by Mugabe's ruling ZANU-PF party -- to block deals regarded by many Zimbabweans as underhand, was undermining confidence among foreign donors, he told Reuters.
Robertson said Zimbabwe was already suffering an image problem compared with neighbouring states such as Mozambique and Zambia that were engaged in sweeping asset sales.
